ProAS: A Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping Framework for Multi-Turn Agentic Reinforcement Learning

Bowen Ding1,2 , Mingda Wan2 , Yuhan Chen2,* , Jiyao Yuan4,† , Qi Zhu4,† , Futing Wang1,2 ,
Heyuan Deng4 , Fei Mi4,‡ , Lifeng Shang4 , Tao Lin2,3,‡ ,
1 Zhejiang University  2 School of Engineering, Westlake University
3 Institute of Advanced Technology, Westlake Institute for Advanced Study
4 Huawei Noah’s Ark Lab
2{dingbowen, wanmingda, wangfuting, lintao}@westlake.edu.cn
4{dengheyuan, mifei2, Shang.Lifeng}@huawei.com
Abstract

Reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for optimizing Large Language Model (LLM) agents, yet efficient critic-free algorithms (e.g., GRPO) suffer from a fundamental uniform credit assignment dilemma that broadcasts trajectory-level advantages equally to all actions. Our analysis reveals that this uniformity inherently reinforces structurally unreasonable actions in preferred trajectories and ignores each action’s downstream deviations in unpreferred ones. To resolve this without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework that leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive experiments across Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct demonstrate that ProAS universally elevates mainstream group-based baselines to new state-of-the-art performance, achieving peak success rates of 91.9% and 94.3% on ALFWorld, alongside 66.7% and 70.8% on WebShop, respectively. Furthermore, it accelerates training convergence by up to 2.44×2.44\times while maintaining strong robustness against imperfect or distilled ARGs. Codes: https://github.com/LINs-lab/ProAS.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that make sequential decisions through interactions with external environments. Their planning and reasoning capabilities have enabled applications in software engineering (?), personal assistance (?), and graphical user interface navigation (?).

Reinforcement Learning (RL) has emerged as the primary paradigm for elevating the agentic capacity of LLMs (??). During RL rollouts, agents generate trajectories composed of interleaved environment states and actions, which introduces a fundamental credit assignment challenge:

Actor-critic algorithms (e.g., PPO (?)) address this by learning a separate critic, which introduces substantial computational overhead and optimization instability in long-horizon settings (??). Conversely, critic-free algorithms like Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) (?) offer computational efficiency by broadcasting a trajectory-level advantage uniformly to every action (?). However, this inherently treats all intra-trajectory actions identically, completely overlooking their critical differences in local validity, task contribution, and downstream influence. As detailed in § 3.2, we term this structural limitation the uniform credit assignment dilemma.

To systematically understand the uniform credit assignment dilemma, we conduct a fine-grained action-intervention analysis (§ 4.2). Our findings reveal a dual suboptimality. First, in preferred trajectories with positive advantages, uniform credit inadvertently reinforces structurally invalid actions (i.e., unreasonable actions) that pollute the context history and impede the agent from reaching success. Second, in unpreferred trajectories with negative advantages, uniform penalization ignores the autoregressive nature of LLMs, where the later deviations may drive from earlier actions. Consequently, they suppress all actions equally but arbitrarily without considering their actual downstream influence.

To resolve this dilemma without introducing critic overhead, we propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS) in § 4.3. ProAS leverages an Agentic Reference Graph (ARG, mentioned in § 4.1), which abstracts task progression into dynamically evolving sub-goals to formally annotate whether an action is reasonable (structurally valid) or progress-advancing (driving task completion). Using these structural annotations, ProAS asymmetrically reshapes trajectory-level advantages in Eq. 7: (1) Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) zeros out the local advantages of unreasonable actions in preferred trajectories to prevent their inadvertent reinforcement. (2) Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR) utilizes Future-Drift (Eq. 6), the inclusive count of downstream non-advancing actions, to assign proportionally heavier penalties to actions triggering severe downstream stagnation.

Extensive experiments in § 6 on ALFWorld (?) and WebShop (?) using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (?) validate ProAS as a versatile, plug-and-play enhancer. It universally elevates mainstream group-based RL baselines (GRPO (?), DAPO (?), GiGPO (?)), boosting success rates by up to 16.7 points (e.g., GRPO on 1.5B ALFWorld) and accelerating training convergence by 1.12×1.12\times to 2.44×2.44\times. On top of that, this orthogonal enhancement propels these standard algorithms to establish new state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance, consistently eclipsing the strong segment-level baseline, MiGPO (?). Notably, GiGPO+ProAS outperforms MiGPO by a massive 13.1 points on WebShop with 1.5B model and secures the highest overall success rate of 94.3% on ALFWorld with 7B model. Furthermore, comprehensive ablations (§ 6.2) show that ProAS’s core mechanisms are both synergistic and superior to alternative advantage shaping variants, and confirm ProAS’s robust efficacy against incomplete or distilled ARGs, underscoring the necessity of ARG’s online evolution mechanism.

In summary, our primary contributions are:

  • •

    Problem Identification: We expose the uniform credit assignment dilemma in critic-free agentic RL, demonstrating how uniform advantages inadvertently reinforce contextual noise in preferred trajectories and ignore the downstream influence of actions in unpreferred ones.

  • •

    Algorithmic Innovation: We propose Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a plug-and-play framework. Guided by a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG), ProAS achieves fine-grained, critic-free credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR).

  • •

    Empirical Superiority: ProAS acts as a universal enhancer across multiple model scales and environments. It significantly accelerates training convergence, propels standard group-based algorithms to surpass strong SOTA baselines (e.g., MiGPO), and exhibits high robustness against imperfect and distilled reference guidance.

2 Related Works

Multi-Turn Agentic Tasks. Large Language Model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed to solve complex real-world tasks (?). Given the intricacies of these environments, agents must engage in multi-turn interactions, continuously accumulating contextual knowledge and making sequential decisions to drive task completion. To facilitate the training and evaluation of such agents, the community has introduced various simulated environments. Examples include ALFWorld (?) for embodied household tasks, WebShop (?) for web navigation, AppWorld (?) for application development, and τ2\tau^{2}-Bench (?) for evaluating dynamic conversational abilities in domains like aviation and retail.

Rather than constructing new environments, our work focuses on developing more efficient and effective training paradigms tailored for existing multi-turn agentic tasks.

RL for LLM Agents. Critic-free RL like GRPO (?) is widely adopted for LLM agents (???), but suffers from sparse-reward advantage vanishment (?) and coarse trajectory-level credit assignment (?). While DAPO (?) and dense-reward methods (???) mitigate this vanishment, their credit assignment remains trajectory-bound. To differentiate intra-trajectory actions, GiGPO (?) and MiGPO (?) compute relative advantages by matching anchor states or milestones across rollouts.

In this work, we systematically expose the flaws of uniform credit assignment in both preferred and unpreferred trajectories, addressing them through advantage shaping, which serves as a plug-and-play module for existing critic-free RL algorithms.

3 Preliminary

3.1 Decision Process of LLM Agents

Given a task context 𝐱∼p⁡(X)\mathbf{x}\sim p(X), an LLM agent aims to solve the task within a maximum horizon of TT steps. At each step t∈[1,T]t\in[1,T], the agent receives an immediate environment state sts_{t}. Governed by a parameterized policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, the agent samples an action ata_{t} from the admissible action space 𝒜\mathcal{A} (?), conditioned on the task context 𝐱\mathbf{x}, the interaction history ht−1={(si,ai)}i=1t−1h_{t-1}=\{(s_{i},a_{i})\}_{i=1}^{t-1}, and the current state sts_{t}. Formally, this decision-making process is defined as:

at∼πθ(⋅∣𝐱,ht−1,st),at∈𝒜,t∈[1,T]a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{x},h_{t-1},s_{t}),\quad a_{t}\in\mathcal{A},\quad t\in[1,T] (1)

In practice, some harnessing wrappers (?) often provide partial observations or integrate summarized historical information (?) (denoted as h^t−1\hat{h}_{t-1}) into the context prior to the current state sts_{t}.

3.2 GRPO

GRPO (?) utilizes a group-level normalization strategy to estimate the advantage for assessing the action value. In GRPO, given a task 𝐱\mathbf{x}, the old policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} generates a group of GG rollout trajectories {τi}i=1G\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}, each evaluated by a verifiable outcome reward R⁡(τi)R(\tau_{i}). The trajectory-level advantage AiA_{i} for τi\tau_{i} is computed by normalizing the rewards within the group:

Ai=R⁡(τi)−μσ+ϵ{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}A_{i}}=\frac{R(\tau_{i})-\mu}{\sigma+\epsilon} (2)

where μ\mu and σ\sigma denote the mean and standard deviation of the group rewards {R⁡(τi)}i=1G\{R(\tau_{i})\}_{i=1}^{G}, and ϵ\epsilon is a small constant ensuring numerical stability. Excluding entropy and KL regularization terms for simplicity, GRPO optimizes the expected trajectory advantage as follows:

𝒥GRPO​(θ)=𝔼𝐱,{τi}i=1G∼πθold​[1G​∑i=1G1|τi|​∑t=1|τi|min⁡(ρi,t​(θ)​Ai,clip⁡(ρi,t​(θ),1−ε,1+ε)​Ai)]\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\,\mathbf{x},\;\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|\tau_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|\tau_{i}|}\min\!\left(\rho_{i,t}(\theta){\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{A}_{i}},\operatorname{clip}\big(\rho_{i,t}(\theta),1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon\big)\,{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{A}_{i}}\right)\right] (3)

where |τi||\tau_{i}| is the trajectory length (in tokens), and yi,ty_{i,t} denotes the tt-th generated token within τi\tau_{i}. The importance ratio ρi,t​(θ)=πθ​(yi,t∣𝐱,yi,<t)πθold​(yi,t∣𝐱,yi,<t)\rho_{i,t}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid\mathbf{x},y_{i,<t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid\mathbf{x},y_{i,<t})} is used in a clipped surrogate with bounds [1−ε,1+ε][1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon] to limit improvements from favorable ratio changes. Differentiating this surrogate gives (see Appx. A):

∇θ𝒥GRPO​(θ)=𝔼𝐱,{τi}i=1G∼πθold​[1G​∑i=1G1|τi|​∑t=1|τi|1i,tclip⋅Ai⋅ρi,t​(θ)⋅∇θ​log​πθ​(yi,t∣𝐱,yi,<t)⏟gradient at step ​(i,t)]\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}}\left[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|\tau_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|\tau_{i}|}\underbrace{\textbf{1}^{\mathrm{clip}}_{i,t}\cdot{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{A}_{i}}\cdot\rho_{i,t}(\theta)\cdot\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid\mathbf{x},y_{i,<t})}_{\text{gradient at step }(i,t)}\right] (4)

where 1i,tclip\textbf{1}^{\mathrm{clip}}_{i,t} indicates whether the surrogate’s gradient is active: it is zero when Ai>0A_{i}>0 and ρi,t>1+ε\rho_{i,t}>1+\varepsilon, or when Ai<0A_{i}<0 and ρi,t<1−ε\rho_{i,t}<1-\varepsilon, and one otherwise, with the boundary convention specified in Appx. A.

Credit Assignment of GRPO. As shown in Eq. 4, the per-step gradient is directly scaled by the credit multiplier 1i,tclip⋅Ai⋅ρi,t​(θ)\textbf{1}^{\mathrm{clip}}_{i,t}\cdot{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{A}_{i}}\cdot\rho_{i,t}(\theta). Under the on-policy setting (where ρi,t​(θ)≡1\rho_{i,t}(\theta)\equiv 1 and thus 1i,tclip≡1\textbf{1}^{\mathrm{clip}}_{i,t}\equiv 1), this multiplier strictly reduces to the trajectory-level advantage Ai{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}{A}_{i}}. Consequently, all steps within the same trajectory are indiscriminately updated by the identical scalar, regardless of their individual difference. We term this systematic limitation the dilemma of uniform credit assignment.

4 Methodology

Since RL fundamentally optimizes policies by incentivizing or suppressing action likelihoods, tailored credit assignment requires understanding both the intrinsic properties of each step (e.g., reasonableness and progress advancement) and how modulating them dictates the final outcome. To quantify these step-level properties, § 4.1 constructs an Agentic Reference Graph (ARG). Guided by an intervention study probing these modulation effects (§ 4.2), § 4.3 introduces Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), a lightweight framework designed to resolve the uniform credit dilemma via asymmetric advantage shaping.

4.1 Agentic Reference Graph

As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), ARG abstracts the task-solving progression into MM ordered sub-goals using pre-collected successful trajectories. Below, we formalize its construction and online evolution, followed by a two-tier annotation scheme to categorize step-level actions.

Construction and Formalization. To ensure reliable action assessment, we enforce strict graph purity by pruning invalid transitions and self-loops (example in Appx. D.3). Furthermore, while sub-goals follow a strict sequence, their internal atomic requirements are often permutation-invariant (example in Appx. D.4). By modeling each sub-goal’s completion as a state equivalence class, we seamlessly unify these diverse execution paths. Formally, the ARG is defined as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ)\mathcal{G}=(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}):

Definition 4.1 (Sub-goals as Vertices).

The vertex set 𝒱=⋃m=1Mgm\mathcal{V}=\bigcup_{m=1}^{M}\textbf{g}_{m} comprises MM sub-goals in sequential order. Each sub-goal gm={sm,1,sm,2,…}\textbf{g}_{m}=\{s_{m,1},s_{m,2},\dots\} is an unordered set of permutation-invariant, valid states, strictly excluding error-induced states and redundant self-loops.

Definition 4.2 (Actions as Edges).

The edge set ℰ⊆⋃m=1M−1(gm×𝒜m×gm+1)\mathcal{E}\subseteq\bigcup_{m=1}^{M-1}(\textbf{g}_{m}\times\mathcal{A}_{m}\times\textbf{g}_{m+1}) captures deterministic transitions (s,a,s′)(s,a,s^{\prime}) between consecutive sub-goals under admissible actions a∈𝒜ma\in\mathcal{A}_{m}.

Dynamic Evolution. To capture the diverse spectrum of valid solutions, the ARG evolves dynamically. Upon verifying a novel successful trajectory at the rollout stage of training iteration kk, we extract its new states (Δ​gm\Delta\textbf{g}_{m}) and actions (Δ​ℰ\Delta\mathcal{E}) to update the current graph 𝒢(k)\mathcal{G}^{(k)} via strict union:

gm(k+1)=gm(k)∪Δ​gm(1≤m≤M),andℰ(k+1)=ℰ(k)∪Δ​ℰ\textbf{g}_{m}^{(k+1)}=\textbf{g}_{m}^{(k)}\cup\Delta\textbf{g}_{m}\quad(1\leq m\leq M),\quad\text{and}\quad\mathcal{E}^{(k+1)}=\mathcal{E}^{(k)}\cup\Delta\mathcal{E} (5)

These discrete updates strictly adhere to the purity principles, providing an increasingly comprehensive reference for action attribution over time (a raw-to-merged example is provided in Appx. D.3).

Action Attribution. We evaluate any rollout trajectory τi={(st,at,st+1)}t=1|τi|\tau_{i}=\{(s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1})\}_{t=1}^{|\tau_{i}|} generated at iteration kk against 𝒢(k)\mathcal{G}^{(k)} to formally annotate each step tt using two binary criteria:

(1) Reasonableness (Reat\text{Rea}_{t}): Evaluates if an action forms a valid ARG transition: Reat=𝕀[(st,at,st+1)∈ℰ(k)]\text{Rea}_{t}=\mathbb{I}[(s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1})\in\mathcal{E}^{(k)}]. While it filters explicit errors, it ignores valid but redundant loops.

(2) Progress-Advancement (PAt\text{PA}_{t}): Strictly quantifies task progression. An action is progress-advancing (PAt=1\text{PA}_{t}=1) if it induces a valid ARG state st+1∈𝒱(k)s_{t+1}\in\mathcal{V}^{(k)} while avoiding the historical trajectory 𝒮≤t={s1,…,st}\mathcal{S}_{\leq t}=\{s_{1},\dots,s_{t}\}: PAt=Reat⋅𝕀[st+1∈𝒱(k)∖𝒮≤t]\text{PA}_{t}=\text{Rea}_{t}\cdot\mathbb{I}\big[s_{t+1}\in\mathcal{V}^{(k)}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{\leq t}\big]

Thus, progress-advancing actions are a strict subset of reasonable ones (PAt\text{PA}_{t} = 1 ⟹\implies Reat\text{Rea}_{t} = 1). Conversely, non-advancing actions (PAt=0\text{PA}_{t}=0) encapsulate both explicit errors and structurally valid but stagnant steps.

4.2 Action-Intervention Analysis

By leveraging the reasonableness and progress-advancement annotations to assess fine-grained action quality, our pilot study reveals how individual steps dictate outcomes, motivating our solution to the uniform credit assignment dilemma.

Probing Unreasonable Actions. Unreasonable actions hinder task progress by polluting the context history and disrupting subsequent decisions (?). Notably, they constitute a substantial proportion of successful GRPO trajectories (41.6% in ALFWorld, 39.6% in WebShop) of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, where they are inadvertently reinforced by the uniform credit applied to preferred rollouts. To probe their impact, we select a clean ALFWorld trajectory (details in Appx. D.1) and sample 50 continuations, {ci}i=150\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{50}, from a fixed state under two context conditions. As illustrated in Fig. 1(b), the clean control retains the original history, whereas the noise-injected condition prepends a four-step unreasonable segment. Despite sharing the identical underlying environment state, this visible context noise degrades the Expected Success Rate (ESR) from 82% to 58%.

Suppressing Actions with Varying Future-Drift. Conversely, non-advancing (NA) actions are heavily concentrated in failed GRPO trajectories (93.1% in ALFWorld, 76.1% in WebShop), where they are suppressed uniformly. Given the autoregressive nature of LLMs, late-stage NA actions are often inevitable consequences of an already polluted context rather than making the mistake independently. Therefore, uniformly suppressing all actions within a failed trajectory is inherently unfair. To quantify the downstream deviation, we define Future-Drift (𝒟i,t\mathcal{D}_{i,t}, short as FD) as the inclusive count of downstream NA actions from step tt in the trajectory τi\tau_{i}, with |τi||\tau_{i}| steps:

𝒟i,t=∑t′=t|τi|(1−PAi,t′)\mathcal{D}_{i,t}=\sum_{t^{\prime}=t}^{|\tau_{i}|}\big(1-\text{PA}_{i,t^{\prime}}\big) (6)

To assess whether actions with higher Future-Drift warrant heavier penalization, we perform a targeted suppression intervention on a failed ALFWorld trajectory generated by Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct as shown in Fig. 1(c). By preserving the trajectory prefix up to specific steps, forbidding the original action, and resampling 50 continuations, we measure the recovered ESR. Suppressing the actions with FD values of 47, 23, 11, and 4 yields ESRs of 24%, 16%, 10%, and 0%, respectively (case details in Appx. D.2). In this case, the higher the suppressed action’s Future-Drift, the more likely the agent is to recover and complete the task.

4.3 Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping

Building upon the empirical insights from § 4.2, we propose the Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS) framework, aiming to resolve the uniform credit dilemma by asymmetrically reshaping the trajectory-level advantage AiA_{i} into a step-wise, progress-aware signal A~i,t\tilde{A}_{i,t}:

A~i,t={Reat⋅Ai,if ​Ai>0,𝒟i,t𝒟¯i+ϵ⋅Ai,if ​Ai<0​ and ​t∈𝒯,Ai,otherwise,\tilde{A}_{i,t}=\begin{cases}\text{Rea}_{t}\cdot A_{i},&\text{if }A_{i}>0,\\ \frac{\mathcal{D}_{i,t}}{\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{i}+\epsilon}\cdot A_{i},&\text{if }A_{i}<0\text{ and }t\in\mathcal{T},\\ A_{i},&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases} (7)

where 𝒯\mathcal{T} denotes the steps sharing the uniform advantage, 𝒟¯i=1|𝒯|​∑t′∈𝒯𝒟i,t′\bar{\mathcal{D}}_{i}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{T}|}\sum_{t^{\prime}\in\mathcal{T}}\mathcal{D}_{i,t^{\prime}} is the average Future-Drift, and ϵ\epsilon ensures numerical stability. This formulation branches into two mechanisms: (1) Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI): Aligning with Insight 1, it zeros out the local advantages of invalid actions (Reat=0\text{Rea}_{t}=0) in preferred trajectories (Ai>0A_{i}>0, usually successful) to prevent inadvertent reinforcement. (2) Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR): Reflecting Insight 2, it leverages normalized Future-Drift to assign proportionally heavier penalties to early pivotal actions in unpreferred trajectories (Ai<0A_{i}<0, usually failed), rectifying the unfairness of uniform suppression.

5 Experimental Setup

To empirically validate the proposed ProAS framework, we conduct extensive experiments across complex, long-horizon agentic environments. Our experiments are structured to answer the following core research questions:

RQ1: Performance & Efficiency (§ 6). Can ProAS consistently elevate task success rates and accelerate training convergence across different model scales under different environments?

RQ2: Algorithm Compatibility (§ 6). Does ProAS seamlessly integrate with mainstream group-based RL baselines (e.g., GRPO, DAPO, GiGPO) as a robust plug-and-play module?

RQ3: Advantage Shaping Design (§ 6.2.1). Are MUI and APR each individually necessary and mutually synergistic, and does ProAS’s Future-Drift-based redistribution outperform a simpler masking heuristic?

RQ4: Robustness to ARG (§ 6.2.2). Does ProAS remain effective when the reference ARG is randomized, incomplete, static (non-evolving), or distilled from a teacher model?

5.1 Models and Data

Models. Our experiments are conducted across two different model scales: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (?), which are denoted as 1.5B and 7B for brevity.

Data. We train and validate on ALFWorld (?) and WebShop (?), two classical long-horizon multi-turn agentic environments (details in Appx. C). ALFWorld is a text-based embodied benchmark over six household task categories (Pick, Look, Clean, Heat, Cool, Pick2, details in Table. 5). Our 150-step training comprises 1777/1767/1784 unique executable tasks of seed 0/1/2 for training and 128 for validation. WebShop (Table 6) is an HTML-based online shopping environment, with 2015/2011/2036 tasks of seed 0/1/2 used for training and 128 for validation.

5.1.1 Evaluation Metrics

Performance Metrics. For ALFWorld, we report the average Success Rate (SR) across the entire validation set, alongside the per-category average SR. For WebShop, we report both the overall average SR and the Task Score (TS). TS is a checklist metric on a scale of 0 to 100: it averages the satisfaction of the requested attributes, options, and price constraint, and then scales this score by how well the purchased product matches the requested product type.

Efficiency Metrics. We quantify training efficiency via speedup Spd@​K=Nbase→K/NProAS→K\text{Spd@}K=N_{\text{base}\to K}/N_{\text{ProAS}\to K}, which is defined as the ratio of RL training steps required by the baseline versus ProAS to first reach a target KK of SR. Reflecting task difficulties, we set K=70%K=70\% for ALFWorld and K=50%K=50\% for WebShop.

5.1.2 Implementation Details

We conduct experiments upon Verl-Agent (?), training all models for 150 RL steps. We validate the policy every 10 RL steps and report metrics from the checkpoint achieving the highest SR. Unless otherwise specified, all experiments are conducted across three random seeds (0, 1, and 2), reporting the mean and sample standard deviation (std). See details in Appx. B.

ARG Initialization. Unless otherwise specified, we initialize the ARG in ALFWorld using its official crowdsourced annotations. Given the strictly sequential nature of tasks in ALFWorld, we formulate each individual step as a distinct sub-goal. For WebShop, the ARG is initialized using its officially annotated sub-goals alongside their corresponding states and actions.

5.1.3 Baselines

We consider baselines of different paradigms: (1) Proprietary models: GPT-5.6-Sol (?), the state-of-the-art model from OpenAI. We apply the reasoning effort as high, and evaluate it with ReAct prompting (?). (2) Prompting: Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, the starting point to be trained. (3) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): Tuning the agent by imitating curated turn-level oracle trajectories from the same training tasks as RL baselines (Details in Appx. B.3). (4) RL: the classical actor-crtic algorithm PPO (?); mainstream group-based RL algorithms GRPO (?), DAPO (?), GiGPO (?); the state-of-the-art (SOTA) agentic RL method MiGPO (?) with segment-level credit assignment.

6 Results and Analysis

6.1 Main Results

Table 1 summarizes the main evaluation results on ALFWorld and WebShop. We structure our analysis to directly address our research questions regarding performance, efficiency (RQ1), and algorithm compatibility (RQ2).

Baseline Comparisons. We first contrast ProAS against established learning paradigms. While both SFT and ProAS leverage expert annotations as supervisory signals, ProAS abstracts them into ARGs to structurally guide RL, significantly outperforming SFT’s direct behavior imitation. Specifically, GiGPO+ProAS achieves 91.9% and 94.3% SR on the 1.5B and 7B ALFWorld benchmarks, respectively, surpassing SFT by 12.2 and 14.4 points. Furthermore, ProAS consistently eclipses PPO, a conventional critic-based RL algorithm, across all settings. ProAS variants outpace PPO by 5.5 to 18.7 points in ALFWorld SR, alongside steady improvements of 4.1 to 12.2 points in WebShop TS and 3.4 to 11.5 points in WebShop SR. Ultimately, these results confirm that explicitly integrating ARG-derived progress signals into RL is vastly superior to both passive trajectory imitation and conventional critic-based credit assignment.

State-of-the-Art Performance. Equipped with ProAS, group-based RL algorithms consistently establish new SOTA records. In ALFWorld, GiGPO+ProAS attains the highest SR of 94.3% on the 7B model. This surpasses the strong segment-level baseline MiGPO and eclipses the proprietary GPT-5.6-Sol by a massive 15.4 points. WebShop presents a notably steeper challenge, evidenced by GPT-5.6-Sol’s severe struggle at 21.9% SR. Despite this difficulty, ProAS variants dominate the leaderboard. On the 1.5B model, both DAPO and GiGPO integrated with ProAS tie for the best SR at 66.7%, outperforming MiGPO by a striking 13.1 points. On the 7B scale, GRPO+ProAS peaks at 70.8%, further extending the lead over MiGPO.

Algorithm Compatibility. Crucially, ProAS demonstrates remarkable plug-and-play compatibility, universally uplifting baseline RL algorithms across all tested configurations. For ALFWorld, equipping GRPO with ProAS yields the most dramatic improvements, boosting the SR by 16.7 points on the 1.5B model and 8.4 points on the 7B model. Consistent gains are mirrored in WebShop, where DAPO+ProAS generates a 9.4-point uplift at the 1.5B scale, and GRPO+ProAS provides a 3.1-point boost at 7B. This confirms ProAS as a versatile enhancer that elevates both the performance floor and ceiling of diverse group-based RL paradigms.

Training Efficiency. Beyond asymptotic performance, ProAS significantly accelerates the training process. On average, it speeds up convergence to target success rates by approximately 1.5×1.5\times for the 1.5B model across both environments. Impressively, this efficiency gain scales favorably with model size: on the 7B model, ProAS accelerates learning by an average of 2.2×2.2\times on ALFWorld and 1.7×1.7\times on WebShop.

6.2 Ablation Study

We ablate the core components of ProAS on the 1.5B model using GRPO as the base algorithm. § 6.2.1 ablates our advantage shaping mechanisms, demonstrating that disabling any single technique lowers the overall success rate and disrupts their synergy. Subsequently, § 6.2.2 relaxes the ARG construction constraints to investigate ProAS’s robustness against reference quality and origin, while highlighting the critical necessity of the online dynamic evolution mechanism.

6.2.1 Advantage Shaping Ablation

To isolate the contributions of our specific advantage shaping interventions, we evaluate five ProAS variants: PR (Progress-aware Reward), ProAS-, ProAS+, ProASmsk±{}_{\text{msk}\pm} and ProASsuffix{}_{\text{suffix}}, as shown in Table 2(a).

First, we contrast advantage shaping against reward shaping. PR incorporates ARG progress annotations directly as an auxiliary step-level reward term rather than reshaping the advantage, as Eq. 14. PR underperforms ProAS by 14.1 and 3.4 SR points on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively. This confirms that explicitly modulating trajectory-level advantages is a superior mechanism for injecting structural progress signals compared to the denser reward design in our studies.

Next, we ablate individual core components, MUI and APR. ProAS- disables MUI on preferred trajectories (Ai>0A_{i}>0), incurring Success Rate (SR) drops of 15.4 and 0.8 points on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively; ProAS+ disables APR on unpreferred ones (Ai<0A_{i}<0), causing a 3.7-point SR drop on ALFWorld and a 1.2-point Task Score (TS) drop on WebShop. These results reveal complementary roles for MUI and APR: MUI prevents reinforcement of unreasonable actions in positively advantaged trajectories, whereas APR differentiates penalties for actions with different Future-Drift in negatively advantaged trajectories. Although their individual benefits vary by environment and metric, both components contribute to ProAS’s overall effectiveness and are jointly essential to its design.

Finally, we evaluate two simpler heuristics for negative trajectories (Ai<0A_{i}<0). ProASmsk±{}_{\text{msk}\pm} preserves MUI but replaces APR by naively masking reasonable actions (Reat=1\text{Rea}_{t}=1) to avoid their suppression, which underperforms ProAS by 14.1 and 0.8 SR points on ALFWorld and WebShop. ProASsuffix{}_{\text{suffix}} replaces the Future-Drift 𝒟i,t\mathcal{D}_{i,t} in Eq.7 with a naive suffix length (𝒟i,tsuffix=|τi|−t+1\mathcal{D}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{suffix}}=|\tau_{i}|-t+1), trailing ProAS by 5.5 and 1.6 SR points. Thus, Future-Drift goes beyond the naive masking and simple positional heuristics. It quantifies each step’s relative responsibility for the penalty, namely its negative credit, and redistributes the penalty accordingly, which drives the superior performance.

Notably, all three variants still outperform native GRPO on the aggregate metrics, highlighting the fundamental necessity of leveraging progress signals to resolve the uniform credit assignment dilemma.

6.2.2 ARG Ablation

Random replaces ARG-derived annotations with random labels instead of matching against the graph. This causes a catastrophic collapse, dropping SR by 39.3 points on ALFWorld and 15.4 points on WebShop relative to ProAS (Table 2(b)). This confirms that clean, ARG-derived annotations are indispensable for accurate credit assignment.

Incomplete randomly prunes 40% of the action-state pairs from the clean ARG to simulate severe degradation. Despite this, ProAS still outperforms GRPO by 7.0 points on ALFWorld. This robustness largely comes from ARG evolution (mentioned in Eq. 5): disabling it (Incomplete&Static) further drops SR by 5.2 points on ALFWorld and 5.4 points on WebShop relative to Incomplete alone. Evolution matters even with a clean ARG, where disabling it (Static) lowers ALFWorld SR from 87.0% (GRPO+ProAS) to 82.8%, though Static still attains the best WebShop SR (65.9%) among all variants. These results confirm the importance of ARG evolution for ProAS, while showing ProAS remains robust to imperfect ARGs.

Distill tests ProAS with synthetic references, since gold-standard trajectories are often unavailable in practice. We prompt a 7B model to generate successful rollouts across training tasks, building a distilled ARG covering 2,566 tasks. With this synthetic ARG, the 1.5B model reaches 83.6% SR on ALFWorld and 64.8% on WebShop, comparable to GRPO+ProAS and 13.3 and 7.8 points above GRPO, respectively. This validates ProAS’s applicability even on teacher-distilled trajectories.

7 Conclusion

In this work, we expose the uniform credit assignment dilemma in critic-free agentic RL, where uniform advantages reinforce contextual noise in preferred trajectories (Ai>0A_{i}>0) and ignore the downstream deviation of actions in unpreferred ones (Ai<0A_{i}<0). To address this without critic overhead, we proposed Progress-Aware Advantage Shaping (ProAS), which leverages a dynamically evolving Agentic Reference Graph (ARG) to achieve fine-grained credit assignment via Masking Unreasonable Incentives (MUI) and Asymmetric Penalty Redistribution (APR). Extensive evaluations across multiple model scales and environments confirm ProAS as a robust, universal enhancer that accelerates convergence and propels mainstream baselines to new state-of-the-art performance. The ablation study further confirms MUI-APR synergy, necessity of ARG evolution and robustness under incomplete or distilled ARGs. Together, these results establish a highly efficient, scalable pathway for elevating autonomous language agents.

Appendix A Derivation of the GRPO Policy Gradient

We derive Eq. 4 from the clipped surrogate in Eq. 3, omitting entropy and KL regularization as in the main text. During each policy update, the sampling policy πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}, sampled trajectories, and group-normalized advantages AiA_{i} are fixed; in particular, ∇θAi=0\nabla_{\theta}A_{i}=0. Let hi,t=(𝐱,yi,<t)h_{i,t}=(\mathbf{x},y_{i,<t}) denote the conditioning context and assume the old policy assigns positive probability to each sampled token.

Clipped token-level surrogate.

Writing ρ=ρi,t​(θ)\rho=\rho_{i,t}(\theta), the contribution of token (i,t)(i,t) is

ℓi,t​(θ)\displaystyle\ell_{i,t}(\theta) =min⁡(ρ​Ai,clip⁡(ρ,1−ε,1+ε)​Ai)\displaystyle=\min\!\left(\rho A_{i},\operatorname{clip}(\rho,1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)A_{i}\right) (8)
={Ai​min⁡(ρ,1+ε),Ai>0,Ai​max⁡(ρ,1−ε),Ai<0,0,Ai=0.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}A_{i}\min(\rho,1+\varepsilon),&A_{i}>0,\\ A_{i}\max(\rho,1-\varepsilon),&A_{i}<0,\\ 0,&A_{i}=0.\end{cases}

Thus, the surrogate is flat only when Ai>0A_{i}>0 and ρ>1+ε\rho>1+\varepsilon, or when Ai<0A_{i}<0 and ρ<1−ε\rho<1-\varepsilon. A ratio outside the clipping interval does not, by itself, imply zero gradient: the gradient remains active when the ratio moves in the unfavorable direction. Away from the clipping boundaries, define

1i,tclip={0,Ai>0​and​ρi,t>1+ε,0,Ai<0​and​ρi,t<1−ε,1,otherwise.\textbf{1}^{\mathrm{clip}}_{i,t}=\begin{cases}0,&A_{i}>0\ \text{and}\ \rho_{i,t}>1+\varepsilon,\\ 0,&A_{i}<0\ \text{and}\ \rho_{i,t}<1-\varepsilon,\\ 1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (9)

At a clipping kink, we adopt the derivative of the active linear branch (indicator 11), a valid generalized-gradient convention. For Ai=0A_{i}=0, the gradient is zero regardless of the indicator.

Since the denominator is fixed, the log-derivative identity gives

∇θρi,t​(θ)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\rho_{i,t}(\theta) =∇θπθ​(yi,t∣hi,t)πθold​(yi,t∣hi,t)\displaystyle=\frac{\nabla_{\theta}\pi_{\theta}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{i,t}\mid h_{i,t})} (10)

Under the usual conditions for exchanging differentiation and expectation, the fixed sampling distribution introduces no additional derivative term. Averaging the token-level derivatives gives

∇θ𝒥GRPO​(θ)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta) =𝔼𝐱,{τi}i=1G∼πθold[1G∑i=1G1|τi|∑t=1|τi|1clipi,tAiρi,t(θ)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x},\{\tau_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}}\Bigg[\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{|\tau_{i}|}\sum_{t=1}^{|\tau_{i}|}\textbf{1}^{\mathrm{clip}}_{i,t}A_{i}\rho_{i,t}(\theta) (12)

which recovers Eq. 4. At θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}, ρi,t=1\rho_{i,t}=1 and the clipping indicator is 11 for ε>0\varepsilon>0. Consequently, all tokens in a trajectory share the same advantage multiplier AiA_{i} (and trajectory normalization 1/|τi|1/|\tau_{i}|), although their score-function gradients can differ. Appendix B Further Implementation Details

B.1 Training Framework

For ALFWorld and WebShop, we adopt the Verl-Agent (?) framework. To ensure robustness and reproducibility, we sample and freeze three distinct training sets with environment seeds 0, 1, and 2 for independent and repeated training. For fair evaluation, all resulting model checkpoints are assessed on a unified, static validation set of 128 tasks. This validation set is strictly disjoint from the training data, rigorously preventing any potential data leakage. Validation uses a temperature of 0.40.4 in both ALFWorld and WebShop.

RL and SFT share the same turn-level input format illustrated in Tables 11 and 12: each prompt contains the task instruction, current observation, admissible actions, and the visible interaction history from the two most recent observation-action turns. The only difference between SFT and RL data is the assistant response, which is curated offline for SFT but generated online for RL.

All experiments are conducted on GPUs. For ALFWorld and WebShop, each 1.5B model run uses 2 GPUs, while each 7B model run uses 4 GPUs.

B.2 RL Configuration

General. We follow the standard Verl-Agent (?) configuration and use the same settings across all RL methods unless otherwise specified. Models are optimized with AdamW using a learning rate of 10−610^{-6}, weight decay 0.010.01, and gradient clipping at 1.01.0. We use a PPO clipping ratio of 0.20.2, an entropy coefficient of 0.0010.001, a KL-loss coefficient of 0.010.01, and one policy-update epoch per rollout batch. At each RL iteration, we sample 16 prompts and generate G=8G=8 trajectories per prompt with temperature 1.01.0 and top-p=1.0p=1.0.

For ALFWorld, we set the maximum prompt and response lengths to 2,048 and 512 tokens, respectively, cap each episode at 50 steps, and use a PPO mini-batch size of 256. For WebShop, the corresponding settings are 4,096 prompt tokens, 512 response tokens, 15 steps, and a PPO mini-batch size of 64.

Reward. Across all runs, we use the same rule-based sparse outcome reward RoR_{\text{o}} in both environments: a successful trajectory receives 1010, whereas an unsuccessful trajectory receives 00. The RoR_{o} is broadcasted into each step in the trajectory. Each invalid action additionally incurs a penalty of −0.1-0.1. Specifically, the response of a step is marked invalid (𝕀⁡[invalid]=1\mathbb{I}[\text{invalid}]=1) if it omits a complete <think>…</think> or <action>…</action> block, or contains Chinese characters, otherwise, the response is valid (𝕀⁡[invalid]=0\mathbb{I}[\text{invalid}]=0). Consequently, the reward for step t′t^{\prime} in trajectory τi\tau_{i} is given by:

Ri,t′=Roi−0.1⋅𝕀⁡[invalidi,t′]R_{i,t^{\prime}}=R_{\text{o}_{i}}-0.1\cdot\mathbb{I}[\text{invalid}_{i,t^{\prime}}] (13)

For progress-aware reward (PR) mentioned in § 6.2.1, we add the progress-aware reward term Rpi,t′=∑t=1t′PAi,t∑t=1|τi|PAi,tR_{\text{p}_{i,t^{\prime}}}=\frac{\sum_{t=1}^{t^{\prime}}\mathrm{PA}_{i,t}}{\sum_{t=1}^{|\tau_{i}|}\mathrm{PA}_{i,t}} for the reward of each step:

Ri,t′=Roi−0.1⋅𝕀⁡[invalidi,t′]+0.5⋅Rpi,t′R_{i,t^{\prime}}=R_{o_{i}}-0.1\cdot\mathbb{I}[\mathrm{invalid}_{i,t^{\prime}}]+0.5\cdot R_{\text{p}_{i,t^{\prime}}} (14)

This design incorporates the progress-advancing information obtained from ARG into the reward signal.

PPO. For PPO (?), we estimate advantages using generalized advantage estimation (GAE) with discount factor γ=1.0\gamma=1.0 and trace-decay parameter λ=1.0\lambda=1.0. We train a separate critic with AdamW using a learning rate of 10−510^{-5} and weight decay 0.010.01, without a critic-only warmup phase. Since PPO does not require multiple rollouts per task for advantage estimation, we sample one rollout per task (G=1G=1) and use a rollout batch of 128 tasks. This matches the 128 sampled trajectories per RL iteration used by the critic-free methods, which sample 8 rollouts for each of 16 tasks. The policy learning rate, regularization, and rollout sampling settings follow the shared configuration above.

DAPO. For DAPO (?), we use asymmetric PPO clipping with lower and upper ratios of 0.20.2 and 0.280.28, respectively, and a dual-clip coefficient of 10.010.0. We disable the actor KL loss and entropy regularization, use token-mean loss aggregation, set the AdamW weight decay to 0.10.1 with 10 learning-rate warmup steps, and disable group filtering.

GiGPO. For GiGPO (?), we set the temporal discount factor to γ=0.95\gamma=0.95 and the step-level advantage weight to 1.01.0. Step advantages are normalized by both the group mean and standard deviation in ALFWorld, and by the group mean only in WebShop.

GiGPO+ProAS. Since GiGPO adopts step-level group-normalized advantages, different steps within the same trajectory need not share the same advantage. This, however, does not affect the plug-in integration of ProAS. We apply MUI to actions with excessively positive advantages, and cluster negative-advantage actions within each trajectory according to their individual advantage magnitudes, rescaling them by future-miss normalization to a mean of one per cluster.

MiGPO. For MiGPO (?), we use mean-normalized segment-level advantages. In ALFWorld, we set the milestone-matching threshold to 0.950.95, the reverse-decay factor to 0.90.9, and the step-level advantage weight to 10.010.0. WebShop uses environment-provided dynamic milestone signals, with a reverse-decay factor of 0.950.95 and a step-level advantage weight of 1.01.0.

B.3 SFT Details

B.3.1 Data Curation.

To construct a controlled imitation-learning baseline matching the RL methods’ task exposure, we curate a supervised dataset for each environment seed (0, 1, 2) from the frozen training tasks:

ALFWorld: We execute the official annotated expert trajectory to obtain one demonstration per unique training game.

WebShop: Lacking official experts, we instantiate a deterministic, goal-conditioned oracle from our ARG using task metadata (target product, query, and options). The resulting trajectories strictly follow the ARG’s sub-goal progression (g1→…→g6\textbf{g}_{1}\rightarrow\dots\rightarrow\textbf{g}_{6}, details in Table 10), explicitly grounding the demonstrations in the same progress structure used by ProAS.

Aligning with the data setting in RL experiments. we represent SFT data as turn-level examples rather than complete trajectories. Each input contains the task instruction, current observation, admissible actions, and the two most recent interaction turns. Table 11 and Table 12 demonstrate the SFT data example of ALFWorld and WebShop.

Training Configuration. We perform full-parameter fine-tuning of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct with the SFT trainer based on FSDP in Verl-Agent, minimizing the token-level negative log-likelihood of the oracle responses. We train for 3 epochs with AdamW (β1=0.9\beta_{1}=0.9, β2=0.95\beta_{2}=0.95), a peak learning rate of 10−510^{-5}, weight decay of 0.010.01, and gradient clipping at 1.01.0. The learning rate follows a cosine schedule with a 3%3\% warmup. We use a maximum sequence length of 4,096 tokens with left truncation and per-GPU micro-batch sizes of 4 and 2 for the 1.5B and 7B models, respectively. We save the checkpoint at the end of each epoch and evaluate every epoch checkpoint on the same frozen 128-task validation set used for RL. The SFT result is reported from the checkpoint with the highest validation success rate.

Appendix C Environment Details

ALFWorld.

ALFWorld (?) is a text-based embodied benchmark built from household tasks in simulated indoor scenes. It covers six task families: single-object manipulation (Pick), object examination (Look), cleaning (Clean), heating (Heat), cooling (Cool), and two-object manipulation (Pick2). At each step, the agent observes textual environment feedback and issues one admissible natural-language action, making ALFWorld a multi-turn, single-step environment. Table 5 reports deduplicated task-family counts for the three frozen training sets and the shared validation set.

WebShop.

WebShop (?) is an HTML-based shopping environment in which the agent must search for a product of Fashion, Garden, Electronics, Grocery and Beauty, then navigate result and product pages, select required options, and purchase the item that matches the user instruction. The task naturally involves both ordered milestones, such as opening the target product before purchasing it, and unordered option choices, such as selecting size and color in either order. Similar to ALFWorld, WebShop allows one environment action per interaction turn. Table 6 reports the distribution of training sets of seed 0/1/2 and the validation set.

C.1 Time Analysis

We compare the wall-clock training time of vanilla RL and RL + ProAS, measured from TensorBoard logs. As shown in Fig. 2, ProAS incurs modest overhead on ALFWorld while achieving lower training time on WebShop. This suggests that ProAS introduces limited computational overhead, as it only requires ARG queries and updates, action-reasonableness checks, and advantage masking and reweighting, without training an additional critic or invoking an extra reward model. The slightly higher training time on ALFWorld may partly reflect its longer interaction horizon, which can accumulate the cost of graph queries, progress assessment, and online graph updates.

Appendix D Case Study

D.1 Unreasonable Action Probing Analysis in ALFWorld

We compare two visible-history conditions while fixing the underlying environment state and rollout budget. Both conditions replay the same three-action clean prefix and reach the same continuation point: the agent is at desk 1, holding keychain 2, with 47 steps remaining. From this state, we independently sample 50 continuations {ci}i=150\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{50} under each condition. In the noise-injected condition, four unreasonable actions are prepended only to the policy-visible interaction history; they are not executed in the continuation environment and therefore do not alter its starting state.

Table 7 first presents the task ARG and then traces the clean and noise-injected conditions separately. Only the four injected unreasonable actions are highlighted in pink. The sampled suffixes are summarized by a continuation row, followed by the Expected Success Rate (ESR) for each condition.

The two panels therefore differ only in the pink history segment; their clean prefix, continuation state, and rollout budget are identical. The observed ESR decrease from 82%82\% to 58%58\% thus diagnoses the effect of unreasonable content in the policy-visible history rather than a change in the underlying environment state.

D.2 Varying Future-Drift Actions Suppression Analysis in ALFWorld

We examine the suppression of four non-advancing actions from the same 50-step failed ALFWorld rollout in Table  8 (c), which are actions of steps 33, 2828, 4040, and 4747. At each position, we preserve the complete preceding prefix, reject only an exact match to the original action, and independently sample 50 continuations {ci}i=150\{c_{i}\}_{i=1}^{50}.

The intervention results exhibit a monotonic relation in this case: the ESR is 24%24\%, 16%16\%, 10%10\%, and 0%0\% when suppressing actions with FD 4747, 2323, 1111, and 44, respectively. The larger recovery at higher-FD positions supports Future-Drift as a diagnostic proxy for an action’s downstream failure burden. Because the four decisions occur at different prefixes and remaining horizons, this case is intended as direct intervention evidence for the diagnostic trend rather than a standalone estimate of a universal causal effect.

D.3 The ARG Dynamic Evolution in ALFWorld

Table 9 illustrates the online ARG evolution mechanism using the task Look at a pencil under the desk lamp. Because the environment’s success criterion broadly accepts any pencil index (e.g., pencil 1 or pencil 2), the task inherently possesses multiple valid solutions that a single static ARG fails to cover. To capture this diversity, any rollout verified as successful during training is first purified by pruning invalid and inadmissible steps. The retained valid path is then seamlessly merged into the current ARG, dynamically expanding its coverage of viable solution trajectories.

D.4 The Order-Agnostic of Actions in WebShop

Table 10 shows a WebShop case from Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct GRPO rollouts. The task-level ARG is ordered across sub-goals, but its option-configuration sub-goal g3\textbf{g}_{3} contains an unordered set of required options. A partial g3\textbf{g}_{3} state satisfies one required option, while g3\textbf{g}_{3} is completed only after all required options are selected. The price and attribute constraints, g4\textbf{g}_{4} and g5\textbf{g}_{5}, are checked at purchase time before the trajectory reaches g6\textbf{g}_{6}.

The contrast highlights the intended granularity of action annotations deriving from ARG. Trajectories A and B differ only within g3\textbf{g}_{3}: they visit different intermediate option states but reach the same completion-state equivalence class, so both option orders are treated as progress-advancing. Trajectory C shows the complementary cases: a wrong option and a premature purchase are unsupported by the ARG, whereas a repeated click on an already selected option can be reasonable but non-advancing. Thus, the ARG preserves ordering constraints among high-level sub-goals while avoiding spurious penalties for valid option permutations.

Appendix E Training Speedup Curves

Fig. 3 visualizes the validation learning curves used to compute the training-speedup results in Table 1. For each base algorithm, speedup is measured by the number of RL steps required to reach a fixed success-rate target before and after adding ProAS.
